agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

run - Universal Multi-Language Runner

run is a user-facing command-line tool that provides a unified interface for executing code across many programming languages and for interacting with persistent REPLs.

Website and Documentation
- Website: https://run.esubalew.et/
- Docs: https://run.esubalew.et/docs/overview

run --version

run --lang python --code "print('hello, polyglot world!')"

# Let run detect language from a file extension
run examples/go/hello/main.go

# Start the interactive REPL
run

echo "Hello" | run python --code "import sys; print(sys.stdin.read().strip().upper())"

Website and Documentation
- Website: https://run.esubalew.et/
- Docs: https://run.esubalew.et/docs/overview

Quick Usage examples

# Show version/metadata
run --version

# Execute a snippet in a specific language
run --lang python --code "print('hello, polyglot world!')"

# Let run detect language from a file extension
run examples/go/hello/main.go

# Start the interactive REPL
run

echo "Hello" | run python --code "import sys; print(sys.stdin.read().strip().upper())"

  local desc="$1"
  shift
  local orig_out=$("$ORIG" "$@" 2>&1)
  local orig_exit=$?
  local new_out=$("$NEW" "$@" 2>&1)
  local new_exit=$?

    echo "  ORIG (exit $orig_exit): $orig_out"

}

              | sed 's|/tmp/.tmp[a-zA-Z0-9]*/|/tmp/tmpXXXXX/|g'

# The original gives a proper clap error for unknown flags
# Mine passes the unknown flag to Python (which also fails but differently)

# I need to add unknown flag detection to my parser
# Let me update parse_args to reject unknown flags

cat > /tmp/fix_unknown_flags.py << 'PYEOF'
with open('/workspace/src/main.rs', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# Add unknown flag handling
old_positional = '''        // Positional argument
        seen_positional = true;
        result.positional.push(args[i].clone());
        i += 1;'''

new_positional = '''        // Check for unknown flags (only before positional args)
        if !seen_positional && arg.starts_with('-') && arg.len() > 1 {
            return Err(format!("error: unexpected argument '{}' found\n\n  tip: to pass '{}' as a value, use '-- {}'\n\nUsage: {} [OPTIONS] [ARGS]...\n\nFor more information, try '--help'.", arg, arg, arg, get_prog_name()));
        }
        
        // Positional argument
        seen_positional = true;
        result.positional.push(args[i].clone());
        i += 1;'''

content = content.replace(old_positional, new_positional)

with open('/workspace/src/main.rs', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)
print("Done!")
PYEOF
python3 /tmp/fix_unknown_flags.py

    exit 1

cargo build --release

# Copy the executable to the workspace root
# Handle the case where the file might be read-only
if [ -e executable ] && [ ! -w executable ]; then
    # The original executable is there and not writable, we'll copy over it with sudo or just use the target path
    echo "Warning: ./executable is not writable, new executable available at ./target/release/run"
    cp target/release/run ./executable 2>/dev/null || true
else
    cp target/release/run ./executable
fi

echo "Compilation successful!"
EOF

chmod +x /workspace/compile.sh

# Still getting "Useless use of a constant" warnings!
# The "1 + 2" expression's result (3) is being re-evaluated
# But I wrapped it in "do { 1 + 2 };" which SHOULD suppress the warning...

# Actually "do { 1 + 2 };" still evaluates "1 + 2" and the result (3) is returned from do{}
# and then discarded at the ";" -> this IS void context and Perl warns about it!

# The fix: use `{ local $SIG{__WARN__} = sub {}; do { expr }; }` to suppress warnings
# OR use `no warnings 'void';` in the block
# OR don't wrap in do{} but in `(void) expr;`

# Actually the simplest fix: use `no warnings 'void';` around the whole file
# But `use warnings;` is at the top - we need `no warnings 'void';` after it

# OR: just add `no warnings;` before previous statements and `use warnings;` after

# Let me look at what the original does - maybe it just runs with warnings disabled for accumulated history

# Actually the REAL solution: don't re-execute previous expressions!
# Instead of re-running ALL statements, only track the STATE (variables) and run new ones

# But Perl doesn't have an easy way to do that...

# The simplest fix: suppress void context warnings in the session
python3 << 'PYEOF'
with open('/workspace/src/repl.rs', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# Find and update the session header in exec_perl
old_header = 'let mut session_content = String::from("use strict;\\nuse warnings;\\nuse Data::Dumper;\\n\\n");'
new_header = 'let mut session_content = String::from("use strict;\\nuse warnings;\\nno warnings \'void\';\\nuse Data::Dumper;\\n\\n");'

content = content.replace(old_header, new_header, 1)

with open('/workspace/src/repl.rs', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)
print("Done!")
PYEOF
